docs.title: Quit Smoking Hub — Data Center
docs.text: The evidence and knowledge infrastructure behind Quit Smoking Hub. Where the main site gives practical knowledge, questions and community experiences, this site provides the structured evidence layer: research records, guidelines, definitions, evidence pages and the community data documentation.

docs.title: What this site is
docs.text:
• Evidence layer: every research record is a published, citable study — never invented, never summarized from memory. See Research.
  • Guideline comparison: what WHO, USPSTF, NICE and the US PHS actually recommend, with dates and differences stated. See Guidelines.
  • Medication and method evidence: per-medication and per-method evidence pages with strength ratings. See Medications and Cessation Methods.
  • Withdrawal science: symptom-by-symptom science — definition, mechanism, timing, what varies, what may help. See Withdrawal.
  • Defined vocabulary: a stable glossary used consistently across both sites. See Definitions.
  • Controversies, stated plainly: e-cigarettes, gradual-vs-abrupt, dual use, medication comparisons. See Controversies.
  • Community data documentation: how the experience database is built, its statistics, and its limits. See Community Data.

docs.text:

The main site links here for evidence; this site links back for practical application. Neither duplicates the other.

docs.title: Evidence integrity rules
docs.text:
1. No fabricated studies, authors, DOIs, PMIDs, statistics or findings. Every record traces to its published source, linked from the record page.
  2. Community experience is not medical evidence. Community data are reported as observations with their own documentation, always separate from the evidence layer.
  3. Uncertainty is stated, not smoothed over. Where evidence conflicts or is insufficient, it says so — see Controversies.
  4. No individual medical advice. Medication pages describe what the evidence shows; they never prescribe.

docs.title: Behaviour Change: The Mechanisms
docs.text: Quitting is a behaviour change problem layered on a pharmacological one. This section covers the behavioural science concepts the platform uses.

docs.title: Cue → routine → reward
docs.text: Most smoking is habitual: a cue (coffee, alcohol, stress, driving) triggers a routine (lighting up) that delivers a reward (nicotine spike + ritual relief). After quitting, the cues remain for months — which is why cravings return in old contexts. The standard strategy is to keep the cue, change the routine, and substitute a reward.

docs.title: Lapse vs relapse — the core distinction
docs.text:
Lapse Relapse Definition A single slip: one or a few cigarettes Return to regular smoking What it means The quit attempt is damaged, not ended The quit attempt has ended Correct response Analyze the trigger, renew the plan, continue quitting Start a new quit attempt — attempt count is not failure

The evidence does not support treating a lapse as catastrophic. People who respond to a slip by recommitting are common among successful long-term quitters — see Relapse section.

docs.title: Self-efficacy
docs.text: Belief in one's ability to quit predicts success in the literature. Self-efficacy is built by surviving high-risk situations without smoking — each survived trigger makes the next one easier. This is why lapse management ("what will I do differently next time") matters more than self-blame.

docs.title: Implementation intentions
docs.text: "If-then" planning ("if I want a cigarette after dinner, then I will brush my teeth immediately") consistently outperforms vague intentions in behaviour-change research. The main site tools page provides practical versions.

docs.title: Why willpower framing is incomplete
docs.text: Quitting framed purely as "willpower" ignores pharmacology (dependence is neurobiological), conditioning (cues fire automatically), and environment (access and social context). The evidence-based framing is: reduce biological demand (medication), reprogramme cues (behaviour change), and change the environment (removing cigarettes, managing triggers). None of these is about moral strength.

docs.title: Three reading rules
docs.text:
1. "Effective" is statistical, not personal. A method that helps more people on average may not be the right one for a given individual.
  2. Combination beats monotherapy. Medication + behavioural support is the single most consistent finding across guidelines.
  3. Community popularity ≠ evidence strength. Cold turkey dominates community reports but is not the most effective aided approach in trials. Both facts can be true — see Community Data.

docs.title: Community Data Center
docs.text: This section of the Data Center documents the structured community experience database that powers the experiential layer of Quit Smoking Hub. It describes where the data comes from, how it is processed, what rules protect privacy and safety, and what the aggregate statistics currently show.

docs.title: What this dataset is
docs.text:
The community experience database is a collection of structured, de-identified records synthesized from real quit-smoking experiences shared in a large public Chinese-language quit-smoking forum (Baidu Tieba's 戒烟吧 / "Quit Smoking Bar"). The forum has operated for nearly two decades and contains tens of thousands of first-person quit accounts, check-in diaries, relapse reports and Q&A threads.

Each record captures, where the source reports it:

  • smoking history (years, cigarettes per day, age group)
  • quit method(s) used
  • recovery stage and day count
  • triggers and cravings
  • physical symptoms and emotional state
  • strategies and interventions
  • outcome and relapse information
  • lessons the person drew

docs.title: What this dataset is not
docs.text:
Community reports are not scientific evidence

Every record is a community report — one person's account of their own experience, as posted in a public forum. The records:

  • are not clinical data and were not medically verified;
  • are not a substitute for research findings, guidelines, or medical advice;
  • may contain selection bias: people who post in a quit-smoking forum are a specific subset of all people who try to quit;
  • cannot support causal claims about any method, symptom, or medication.

Aggregate statistics below describe what this forum's members reported, nothing more.

docs.title: Privacy and ethics rules
docs.text:
The ingestion pipeline follows these rules, which are enforced for every record:

  1. No usernames, user IDs, avatars, or contact information are ever stored or published.
  2. No verbatim copying or wholesale translation of any post — records are original English editorial syntheses of the reported facts.
  3. Unreported fields are marked "Not reported" — nothing is inferred to fill gaps.
  4. Thin records (insufficient information) remain in the internal database and are marked noindex; they generate no public pages.
  5. Medical safety gate: content indicating mental-health high risk (e.g. self-harm, crisis) is held in review status and never auto-published.
  6. Non-judgmental language: the site uses "relapse" and "return to smoking", never "failure" or "weakness".

docs.title: Where the records live
docs.text:
The full structured records are maintained in the main site's content repository (SmokingCessation, src/data/experiences/, src/data/relapse/, src/data/patterns/). Public pages render at:

  • Community Experiences — individual experience pages
  • Relapse Reports — structured relapse records
  • Community Patterns — patterns observed across multiple reports

See also the ingestion pipeline documentation (CONTENT-INGESTION.md) and the data model (DATA-MODEL.md).

docs.title: Smoking history reported
docs.text:
• 70 of 133 published records (53%) report years of smoking; the rest are marked "Not reported".
  • Reported histories range from 3 to 40 years; 39 records fall in the 10–20 year range and 25 in the 21–40 year range.
  • Age groups reported: 20s (7), 30s (7), 40s (3), 50s (1) — most records do not state age.
  • Gender reported: female (2) — most records do not state gender.

docs.title: Relapse
docs.text:
• 13 of 133 published experience records (10%) describe at least one previous relapse.
  • The 12 structured relapse reports record time smoke-free before relapse:
Time smoke-free before relapse Reports 2–3 months 5 100 days 1 6 months 1 7 months 2 9 months 1 1 year 1 1.5 years 1 ~4 years 1

One structured report spans two relapses (6 months, then 3 months) and appears in both rows. Beyond the structured reports, one published experience (EXP-2020-005) records a quit of roughly 1,730 days — nearly five years — that was lost, followed by a new attempt: the longest relapse-free period documented in the database.

docs.title: Patterns observed across reports
docs.text:
1. Alcohol and social occasions — the most reported relapse setting (6 relevant reports), including one report of surviving drinking situations smoke-free (a contradictory case).
  2. Relapse returns a heavier habit — several reports describe smoking more after relapse than before the quit (3 relevant reports).
  3. The first cigarette is the relapse — a single cigarette taken as reward or accepted casually was the pivot point of relapse in multiple reports (6 relevant reports), including two near-miss cases in which the slip was contained and the quit continued.
  4. Smoking dreams — vivid dreams about smoking, usually arriving around a month into the quit and treated by reporters as a passing phase rather than a warning (3 relevant reports; none relapsed).
  5. Health events as the decisive motivation — quits started from a hospitalization, diagnosis, a relative's smoking-related death or alarming test results, described as feeling different from gradual decisions (9 relevant reports).
  6. Daily check-ins as a commitment device — daily sign-in rituals maintained for years, in two cases a decade, with the streak and its public visibility anchoring the quit (6 relevant reports).

docs.title: How these numbers change
docs.text:
Statistics are recomputed after each ingestion batch. Each batch:

  1. collects source material only from real, public forum posts;
  2. applies the privacy filter and de-identification rules;
  3. structures records against the published data model;
  4. deduplicates against existing records;
  5. writes an original English editorial synthesis (no verbatim translation);
  6. assigns quality score, confidence level, and editorial status (published / noindex / review);
  7. rebuilds the site — noindex and review records never produce public pages.

docs.title: Controversies
docs.text: Topics where the published evidence genuinely conflicts, is contested, or remains insufficient. This section presents positions as they are actually held — by named guidelines and studies — without taking sides. Controversies are not manufactured: each topic here has real divergence in the literature or among major guideline bodies.

docs.title: Current topics
docs.text:
1. E-cigarettes for smoking cessation — Cochrane finds high-certainty evidence they help people quit; WHO and USPSTF decline to recommend them; NICE explicitly allows offering them. Long-term safety unknown.
  2. Gradual reduction vs abrupt quitting — the Cochrane evidence says supported gradual and abrupt quitting produce similar quit rates; community experience strongly favors cold turkey; the public debate persists.
  3. Dual use (smoking + vaping) — is it a bridge to quitting or a trap that sustains smoking?
  4. Medication comparisons — varenicline vs cytisine vs NRT combinations: what the network meta-analyses actually say.

docs.title: Reading rules for this section
docs.text:
• Every position is attributed and dated.
  • "Evidence supporting" and "evidence against / limitations" are listed separately.
  • Where guidelines disagree, the disagreement is stated flatly — the platform does not arbitrate.
  • This is not a list of "both sides" of settled questions. Settled questions (e.g., whether smoking causes cancer) are not controversies.

docs.title: Dual Use: Smoking + Vaping
docs.text: Using e-cigarettes while still smoking cigarettes. Positioned by some as a transition stage; by others as a trap.

docs.title: Evidence supporting dual use as a bridge
docs.text:
• In observational data, some dual users later transition to exclusive vaping or quit entirely; vaping reduces cigarette consumption for some.
  • Harm-reduction logic: fewer cigarettes smoked means lower (not zero) toxicant exposure, and NRT harm-reduction precedents exist.

docs.title: Evidence against / limitations
docs.text:
• Most dual users remain dual users — in several cohort studies the majority do not quit smoking within follow-up.
  • Continued smoking keeps most smoking-related risk; harm reduction requires actually stopping cigarettes.
  • Nicotine intake can be higher during dual use than while smoking alone, prolonging dependence.
  • WHO cautions that dual use can sustain smoking rather than end it.

docs.title: What is known vs uncertain
docs.text:
• Known: dual use reduces harm only insofar as it reduces cigarette consumption; it does not eliminate smoking risk; many dual users do not transition.
  • Uncertain: how often dual use is a genuine stepping stone versus a lasting state; long-term outcomes.

docs.title: Platform treatment
docs.text: Community records that describe dual use are reported as experiences. The platform's position: the goal is stopping combustible cigarettes; dual use is at best an unstable intermediate state, and anyone dual-using is encouraged to set a date to stop cigarettes completely.

docs.title: E-Cigarettes for Smoking Cessation
docs.text: The single largest controversy in cessation. The evidence is strong in one direction and the guidelines genuinely split.

docs.title: Evidence supporting e-cigarettes as cessation aids
docs.text:
• Cochrane living review (2024 update, R-013): high-certainty evidence that nicotine e-cigarettes increase quit rates compared with NRT; moderate-certainty evidence versus behavioural support or no support. This upgraded earlier (moderate) certainty ratings.
  • Hajek et al., NEJM 2019 (R-005): in a UK stop-smoking service, e-cigarette users achieved roughly double the 1-year abstinence of NRT users (18.0% vs 9.9%).
  • NICE NG209: clinicians may offer nicotine-containing e-cigarettes to people interested in using them to quit, with advice to stop smoking completely.

docs.title: Evidence against / limitations
docs.text:
• Long-term safety is unknown. E-cigarettes are a relatively new product class; decades-long outcomes do not exist. Non-nicotine constituents (flavourings, aerosol byproducts) are under active study.
  • WHO (2024): does not recommend e-cigarettes as cessation aids, citing insufficient evidence of safety and effectiveness at population level; notes industry involvement in the market.
  • USPSTF (2021): I statement — evidence insufficient to assess the balance of benefits and harms; directs clinicians to interventions with proven effectiveness.
  • Youth uptake concern: non-smoking young people who vape are at higher risk of later cigarette smoking in observational studies — a public-health harm independent of any cessation benefit.
  • Dual use is common and its net effect is debated (see dual-use).

docs.title: Guideline positions (as published)
docs.text: Body Position Cochrane (evidence body) High-certainty evidence of efficacy vs NRT NICE NG209 (UK) May be offered as a cessation aid WHO 2024 Not recommended as cessation aid USPSTF 2021 (US) Evidence insufficient (I)

docs.title: What is known vs uncertain
docs.text:
• Known: nicotine e-cigarettes outperform NRT in randomized trials for quitting; they are not harmless; they are inappropriate for non-smokers, especially youth.
  • Uncertain: long-term health effects; net population impact; optimal role relative to approved medications.

docs.title: Platform position
docs.text: The platform treats e-cigarettes as experimental-adjacent but trial-supported — stronger than "unproven", weaker than approved medications, and never for non-smokers. Community reports of vaping-assisted quits are recorded in the experience database without endorsement.

docs.title: Gradual Reduction vs Abrupt Quitting
docs.text: A public debate with a surprisingly clear evidence picture — and a notable community-vs-trial divergence.

docs.title: What the evidence says
docs.text:
• Cochrane R-004 (Lindson-Hawley et al.): among people who want to quit, quitting abruptly and quitting by gradual reduction with support produce similar long-term quit rates. Gradual reduction without any support is less well evidenced.
  • NICE NG209 supports staged reduction with temporary use of licensed nicotine products for people not ready to stop in one go.
  • The old folk belief that "cutting down first weakens the attempt" is not supported by the trial literature.

docs.title: Why the debate persists
docs.text:
• Community experience skews cold turkey. In the platform's own experience database, cold turkey is by far the most reported method (see community statistics), and many long-term quitters credit the clean break.
  • Selection effect: people who choose cold turkey may differ from those who choose reduction (motivation, dependence, support). Observational popularity does not prove comparative effectiveness.
  • "Gradual" means different things: self-managed cutting-down versus supported reduction with NRT are different interventions with different evidence.

docs.title: What this means practically
docs.text: Both routes are legitimate. The evidence-backed advice is: whichever route, set a fixed quit date and use the strongest support available — the difference between methods is smaller than the difference between supported and unsupported attempts.

docs.title: Positions
docs.text:
• Trial literature: no meaningful difference when both are supported.
  • Community experience: strong preference for abrupt, often credited with success.
  • Platform: presents both, treats the community preference as a reported pattern, not proof of superiority.

docs.title: Medication Comparisons: What the Network Meta-Analyses Say
docs.text: The comparative evidence on cessation medications, from the Cochrane network meta-analysis tradition.

docs.title: The main comparisons
docs.text:
• Varenicline vs NRT monotherapy: varenicline generally emerges as the more effective single agent in network meta-analyses (R-008; Cochrane partial-agonists review R-002).
  • Varenicline vs bupropion: varenicline generally superior on quit rates (R-002, R-008).
  • Cytisine vs NRT: Walker 2014 (R-017) found cytisine noninferior-to-superior at 1 month, with the difference narrowing and becoming non-significant at 6 months — at much lower cost. Cochrane partial-agonists analyses include cytisine (R-002).
  • Cytisine vs varenicline: fewer head-to-head trials; both are partial agonists; varenicline has the larger trial base.
  • Combination NRT (patch + fast-acting form): more effective than single-form NRT (R-008) — the standard advice in UK services.
  • E-cigarettes vs NRT: high-certainty evidence favors nicotine e-cigarettes (R-013) — but see the e-cigarettes controversy for the full picture.

docs.title: What is genuinely uncertain
docs.text:
• Whether cytisine fully matches varenicline in direct comparison (ongoing trials).
  • Optimal duration of treatment.
  • Which medication is best for specific subgroups (heavy smokers, psychiatric comorbidity, pregnancy — USPSTF marks pregnancy pharmacotherapy as an I statement).

docs.title: Reading note
docs.text: "More effective on average" is not "better for you". Choice involves cost, availability, side-effect profile, prior experience and preference — which is why every medication page here ends with questions for a healthcare professional, and why this platform never ranks medications for individuals.

docs.title: Definitions
docs.text: The glossary of defined terms used across this platform. Each definition is written to be clear, stable, and consistent between the main site and the data site. Where a term has a formal technical meaning, the plain-language version is given first.

docs.title: Core terms
docs.text: Term Definition Abstinence Sustained non-smoking over a defined period (e.g., continuous abstinence since a quit date). Craving An intense urge to smoke; has a pharmacological component (nicotine-adapted brain) and a conditioned component (triggers). Trigger A cue — internal (stress, alcohol, boredom) or external (coffee, driving, social events) — that activates the urge to smoke. Withdrawal The symptom syndrome that follows nicotine removal as the brain and body re-adapt; peaks in week 1, mostly resolves in 2–4 weeks. Lapse A single slip — one or a few cigarettes after a quit date. Not the end of the quit attempt. Relapse Return to regular, ongoing smoking; the quit attempt has ended. Quit attempt A deliberate, dated attempt to stop smoking, regardless of outcome. Quit date The planned day smoking stops. Nicotine dependence Neuroadaptation to nicotine producing craving, tolerance and withdrawal on removal. NRT Nicotine replacement therapy: patch, gum, lozenge, inhaler or spray delivering nicotine without tobacco smoke. Cold turkey Stopping smoking abruptly, without medication or gradual reduction. Gradual reduction Tapering cigarette consumption before a quit date, with or without nicotine products. Harm reduction Strategies to reduce harm without full abstinence (e.g., switching to lower-risk nicotine products); distinct from cessation. Dual use Using e-cigarettes or other products while still smoking cigarettes. Evidence strength Grading of a research record: Strong / Moderate / Limited, based on design and consistency.

Community reports… Observation drawn from the de-identified experience database — not medical evidence. What remains uncertain… Genuine gaps or conflicts in the published evidence.

docs.title: Clinical & Public Health Guidelines
docs.text:
Structured comparison of authoritative cessation guidelines. Every entry records the issuing body, year, scope, key recommendations and where the guidelines differ. Sources are Tier-1: WHO, national health agencies and independent guideline bodies.

Rule: guideline positions are reported as published, with the guideline date stated. Positions are never paraphrased into stronger or weaker claims than the source makes.

docs.title: Guideline comparison at a glance
docs.text: Body Document Year Pharmacotherapy position Behavioural support E-cigarettes WHO Clinical treatment guideline for tobacco cessation in adults 2024 Recommends varenicline, NRT, bupropion, cytisine Strongly recommended (brief advice + intensive support) No recommendation for cessation use; evidence insufficient USPSTF (US) Tobacco Smoking Cessation in Adults, Including Pregnant Persons 2021 Recommends FDA-approved pharmacotherapy for nonpregnant adults (A) Recommends behavioural interventions (A) Evidence insufficient (I statement) NICE (UK) NG209 Tobacco: preventing uptake, promoting quitting and treating dependence 2021 (last reviewed 2025) Recommends varenicline, NRT, bupropion, cytisine options Behavioural support for all, intensively for some Nicotine-containing e-cigarettes can be offered as an aid US PHS Treating Tobacco Use and Dependence: 2008 Update 2008 First-line: 7 approved medications Counseling + medication combined recommended Predates modern evidence base

docs.title: Records
docs.text:
• WHO 2024 — clinical treatment guideline
  • USPSTF 2021 — recommendation statement
  • NICE NG209 — tobacco dependence guideline
  • US PHS 2008 — Treating Tobacco Use and Dependence

docs.title: How to read these records
docs.text: Guidelines are statements by specific bodies at specific dates. They can and do differ — on e-cigarettes, on medication ordering, and on how strongly behavioural support is emphasized. Differences usually reflect different evidence cut-off dates, different regulatory contexts and different risk tolerances, not scientific disagreement about core facts. Where positions differ, this site states the difference rather than picking a winner.

docs.title: NICE NG209 — Tobacco: preventing uptake, promoting quitting and treating dependence
docs.text: Field Value Issuing body National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (UK) Year 2021; last reviewed 4 February 2025 Scope Support to stop smoking for everyone aged 12 and over; harm reduction; prevention of uptake in children, young people and young adults (up to 24) Source nice.org.uk/guidance/ng209

docs.title: Key positions
docs.text:
• Behavioural support: individual or group behavioural support should be offered to everyone who wants to quit; it should not be rationed by "readiness to quit".
  • Medications: varenicline and NRT (alone or combined) are the principal options; bupropion and cytisine are also covered — the 2025 review added new recommendations on cytisinicline (cytisine).
  • E-cigarettes: clinicians can offer nicotine-containing e-cigarettes as an aid for people interested in using them to quit smoking; users should be advised to stop smoking completely.
  • Harm reduction: for people not ready to stop in one go, supports staged reduction, including temporary use of licensed nicotine products.

docs.title: Notable differences
docs.text: NG209 is the most e-cigarette-accommodating of the major guidelines: it treats nicotine-containing e-cigarettes as a legitimate offer, in contrast to WHO (insufficient evidence) and USPSTF (I statement). NG209 also explicitly addresses harm reduction and gradual approaches, and extends to people aged 12 and over.

docs.title: US PHS 2008 — Treating Tobacco Use and Dependence: 2008 Update
docs.text: Field Value Issuing body US Public Health Service (Clinical Practice Guideline) Year 2008 (updated from 2000) Scope Clinical treatment of tobacco dependence in adults Source Treating Tobacco Use and Dependence: 2008 Update (AHRQ)

docs.title: Key positions (as published in 2008)
docs.text:
• Tobacco dependence is a chronic condition that often requires repeated intervention.
  • Counselling and medication are each effective; combining them is more effective than either alone.
  • Seven first-line medications were identified as effective: five NRT forms (gum, patch, lozenge, inhaler, nasal spray), bupropion SR and varenicline.
  • Clinicians should use the 5 A's model: Ask, Advise, Assess, Assist, Arrange follow-up.
  • Quitlines (e.g., 1-800-QUIT-NOW in the US) are effective and should be promoted.

docs.title: Status today
docs.text: The 2008 guideline is the classic US reference but predates: the EAGLES safety trial (2016), cytisine trials, the e-cigarette evidence base and the 2020 Surgeon General report. It remains cited here because its central findings — dependence is chronic, treatment works, combination beats monotherapy — remain the foundation of every later guideline. For current US recommendations see USPSTF 2021.

docs.title: USPSTF 2021 — Interventions for Tobacco Smoking Cessation in Adults, Including Pregnant Persons
docs.text: Field Value Issuing body U.S. Preventive Services Task Force Year 2021 Publication JAMA 2021;325(3):265-279 DOI 10.1001/jama.2020.25019 PMID 33464343

docs.title: Recommendations
docs.text:
• Nonpregnant adults (A recommendation): clinicians should ask all adults about tobacco use, advise stopping, and provide behavioural interventions and FDA-approved pharmacotherapy.
  • Pregnant persons (A recommendation): clinicians should ask about tobacco use, advise stopping, and provide behavioural interventions.
  • Pharmacotherapy in pregnancy (I statement): evidence insufficient to assess balance of benefits and harms.
  • E-cigarettes (I statement): evidence insufficient to assess benefits and harms for cessation in adults; clinicians should direct patients to interventions with proven effectiveness.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The USPSTF position is the reference US preventive-care statement. Its A-grade recommendations mean high certainty of substantial net benefit. The two I statements mark genuine evidence gaps — not "no benefit", but "not yet proven" — which is why this site keeps e-cigarettes in the Controversies section rather than in Methods.

docs.title: WHO clinical treatment guideline for tobacco cessation in adults (2024)
docs.text: Field Value Issuing body World Health Organization (WHO) Year 2024 (first-ever WHO clinical guideline on tobacco cessation) Scope Adults using any tobacco product: cigarettes, waterpipes, smokeless tobacco, cigars, roll-your-own, heated tobacco products Basis GRADE evidence reviews Source WHO publication 9789240096431

docs.title: Key recommendations
docs.text:
• Behavioural support: brief advice (30 seconds to 3 minutes) should be offered to every tobacco user in health settings; more intensive individual, group or telephone counselling should be offered where feasible.
  • Digital interventions: digital cessation interventions can be offered as complements to other support.
  • Pharmacotherapy (adults): recommends varenicline, nicotine replacement therapy (NRT), bupropion and cytisine as effective cessation medications. Choice should consider the user's medical context, preferences and availability.
  • Combination: behavioural plus pharmacological treatment is recommended over either alone.
  • Smokeless tobacco: specific recommendations for cessation of smokeless tobacco products are included.

docs.title: Notable context
docs.text:
• The guideline is written for health-care providers and for health-system managers; it is designed to be implementable in low-resource settings.
  • WHO notes that in 2023 it initiated a prequalification procedure for cessation medications, and that NRT products were first prequalified in April 2024.
  • On e-cigarettes: WHO states the current evidence is insufficient to recommend them as cessation aids at population level, while acknowledging that individual countries regulate them differently.

docs.title: Differences from other guidelines
docs.text: Compared with NICE NG209 (UK), WHO is more cautious about e-cigarettes as cessation aids. Compared with USPSTF 2021, WHO explicitly includes cytisine, which is not FDA-approved in the US. All three agree on the core: offer behavioural support plus pharmacotherapy.

docs.title: Health Effects: What Smoking Does and What Quitting Changes
docs.text: The evidence layer on harm and recovery. The body-recovery timeline on the main site is the practical version of this page.

docs.title: The core evidence
docs.text:
• Smoking is causally linked to cancer, cardiovascular disease, respiratory disease, and many other conditions — the causal framework is documented across Surgeon General reports and WHO reports spanning decades.
  • The landmark Jha et al. study of ~200,000 US adults found: quitting before age 40 avoids most of the excess mortality of continued smoking; quitting between 25–34 adds roughly a decade of life; quitting at any age confers benefit — see R-006.

docs.title: What happens after quitting (documented averages)
docs.text:
Timeframe Documented change 20 min Heart rate and blood pressure begin to drop 12–24 h Carbon monoxide clears from blood Weeks Circulation and lung function improve; coughing may transiently increase as cilia recover 1–9 months Cilia function recovers; cough and shortness of breath typically decrease 1 year Excess coronary heart disease risk roughly halves 5 years Stroke risk approaches that of a non-smoker 10+ years Lung cancer risk falls substantially; risks keep declining

These are population averages summarized from US Surgeon General and WHO materials; individual outcomes vary.

docs.title: What the community reports
docs.text: Community experiences in the database frequently describe easier breathing within weeks, taste and smell returning within days, and energy improvements over months. These reports are consistent with the evidence — they are not themselves evidence, and individual absence of noticeable benefit does not mean absence of biological recovery.

docs.title: What does NOT happen
docs.text:
• No health effect appears instantly reversible at the moment of the last cigarette.
  • Quitting does not erase all accumulated risk; it substantially reduces future additional risk.
  • Harm reduction products (e-cigarettes) are covered under Controversies — long-term safety is genuinely uncertain.

docs.title: Cessation Medications
docs.text:
Evidence pages for the medications with the strongest published evidence: nicotine replacement therapy (NRT), varenicline, bupropion and cytisine. Each page reports what the medication is, how it works, what trials and systematic reviews show, common considerations, and questions to ask a healthcare professional.

This is medication information, not medical advice and not prescriptions. Dosing, suitability and interactions are individual clinical decisions. Any medication can have side effects; none of these pages substitutes for discussion with a prescriber or pharmacist.

docs.title: What it is
docs.text: A prescription medication (bupropion SR; also marketed as an antidepressant under other brand names) used for smoking cessation. It is not nicotine-based.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text: Its exact mechanism in cessation is not fully understood. It affects dopamine and noradrenaline pathways implicated in reward and withdrawal, and appears to reduce craving and withdrawal symptoms.

docs.title: What the evidence shows
docs.text:
• The Cochrane review of antidepressants for smoking cessation found bupropion approximately doubles quit rates versus placebo — see R-003.
  • In EAGLES, bupropion showed no significant increase in moderate-to-severe neuropsychiatric adverse events versus placebo — see R-015.
  • WHO (2024), USPSTF (2021) and NICE (NG209) all include bupropion among recommended options; it is often the choice when varenicline is unavailable or unsuitable.

docs.title: Common considerations
docs.text:
• Insomnia and dry mouth are commonly reported.
  • Bupropion lowers seizure threshold; it is not used in people with seizure disorders, eating disorders with purging, or certain other conditions — suitability is a clinical decision.
  • It can be combined with NRT in some protocols; ask about combined treatment.

docs.title: Questions to ask a healthcare professional
docs.text:
• Do any of my conditions or medications interact with bupropion?
  • What should I do if sleep becomes difficult after starting?
  • Is combining bupropion with NRT appropriate for me?

Related: Varenicline · NRT · Research record R-003

docs.title: What it is
docs.text: A plant-derived partial agonist at nicotinic receptors — pharmacologically a cousin of varenicline, but far older and far cheaper. It has been used for smoking cessation in Eastern Europe for decades; a modernized form (cytisinicline) is under development.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text: Like varenicline, it partially activates nicotinic receptors, easing withdrawal while reducing the reward from smoking. Treatment courses are typically short — about 25 days with a tapering tablet schedule.

docs.title: What the evidence shows
docs.text:
• West et al. (NEJM 2011): cytisine significantly increased 12-month abstinence versus placebo (8.4% vs 2.4%) — see R-016.
  • Walker et al. (NEJM 2014): at 1 month, cytisine outperformed NRT (40% vs 31%); by 6 months the difference narrowed (22% vs 15%) and was not statistically significant, at a fraction of NRT's cost — see R-017.
  • Cochrane's partial-agonists review covers cytisine within its scope — see R-002.
  • WHO (2024) recommends cytisine; NICE added cytisinicline recommendations in its 2025 review. Cytisine is not FDA-approved in the US, so USPSTF's US recommendation set does not include it.

docs.title: Common considerations
docs.text:
• Dry mouth and gastrointestinal symptoms are commonly reported; side effects are generally mild and self-limiting.
  • Cost is the standout feature: cytisine courses cost a small fraction of varenicline or NRT in most markets, which is why WHO emphasizes it for global access.
  • Availability is the main practical barrier in countries where it is not licensed.

docs.title: Questions to ask a healthcare professional or pharmacist
docs.text:
• Is cytisine available and licensed where I live?
  • Does the short course fit my situation, or would a longer treatment be better?
  • How does cytisine compare with varenicline for me?

Related: Varenicline · NRT · WHO 2024 guideline

docs.title: What it is
docs.text: NRT supplies nicotine without tobacco smoke, in controlled doses, through a patch, gum, lozenge, inhaler or nasal spray. The patch provides slow, steady delivery; gum and lozenge deliver faster, on-demand relief.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text: It reduces withdrawal symptoms and cravings while the person breaks the behavioural habit of smoking. Because the dose is lower and delivered without the rapid nicotine spike of a cigarette, dependence is typically easier to step down.

docs.title: What the evidence shows
docs.text:
• The Cochrane review of NRT (Stead et al.) found NRT in any form increases quit rates by roughly 50–70% versus placebo — see R-001.
  • In the EAGLES trial, the nicotine patch showed no increase in moderate-to-severe neuropsychiatric adverse events versus placebo — see R-015.
  • WHO (2024), USPSTF (2021) and NICE (NG209) all recommend NRT; in the UK, combining a patch with a fast-acting form (gum or lozenge) is standard practice.

docs.title: Common considerations
docs.text:
• Local irritation (patch), jaw discomfort (gum), throat/mouth irritation (lozenge) are commonly reported and usually mild.
  • Vivid dreams or disturbed sleep can occur with 24-hour patch use; many people remove the patch at night.
  • NRT is widely available without prescription in many countries, which makes it the most accessible first-line option.

docs.title: Questions to ask a healthcare professional
docs.text:
• Which form or combination suits my smoking pattern?
  • How long should I continue NRT, and how should I taper?
  • Are there reasons NRT is less suitable for me (pregnancy, cardiovascular history, recent heart attack)?

Related: Bupropion · Cytisine · Withdrawal science

docs.title: What it is
docs.text: A prescription medication (marketed as Chantix/Champix) developed specifically for smoking cessation. It is a partial agonist at nicotinic acetylcholine receptors.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text: It binds to the same brain receptors as nicotine. It partially stimulates them — reducing withdrawal and craving — while blocking nicotine from fully activating them, which reduces the reward of smoking.

docs.title: What the evidence shows
docs.text:
• Cochrane's review of nicotine receptor partial agonists found varenicline increases quit rates substantially versus placebo (roughly 2–3x) — see R-002.
  • The EAGLES trial (8,144 participants, with and without psychiatric disorders) found no significant increase in moderate-to-severe neuropsychiatric adverse events versus placebo or patch, and varenicline was the most effective of the compared treatments — see R-015.
  • The 2016 network meta-analysis overview placed varenicline among the most effective single medications — see R-008.
  • WHO (2024), USPSTF (2021) and NICE (NG209) all recommend varenicline.

docs.title: Common considerations
docs.text:
• Nausea is the most commonly reported side effect, usually mild and early in treatment.
  • Abnormal dreams and insomnia are also commonly reported.
  • Following the EAGLES results, regulators removed the black-box neuropsychiatric warning. People with a history of psychiatric illness were included in the trial; individual assessment still matters.
  • Availability varies by country and by supply history; generic forms exist in several markets.

docs.title: Questions to ask a healthcare professional
docs.text:
• Is varenicline suitable given my medical history and current medications?
  • What should I expect in the first weeks, and what side effects should I report?
  • How does it compare with NRT or cytisine for me specifically?

docs.title: Nicotine: What It Is and How Dependence Works
docs.text: Understanding nicotine is the foundation of understanding quitting. This page covers the pharmacology — what nicotine does in the brain, why dependence develops, and why withdrawal happens.

docs.title: What nicotine is
docs.text: Nicotine is the primary addictive substance in tobacco. It is a stimulant alkaloid that reaches the brain within seconds when inhaled in cigarette smoke — faster than intravenous administration.

docs.title: How dependence develops
docs.text:
• Nicotine binds to nicotinic acetylcholine receptors, releasing dopamine in reward pathways. The fast spike and rapid clearance of cigarette-delivered nicotine makes the reinforcement loop unusually strong.
  • With repeated use, the brain adapts: receptor numbers change, and normal function comes to depend on nicotine. This is neuroadaptation — the biological core of dependence.
  • Behavioural conditioning then layers on top: lighting up becomes paired with coffee, driving, stress, alcohol, work breaks. The habit network is what keeps triggering urges long after the biology settles.

docs.title: Why withdrawal happens
docs.text:
When nicotine is removed, the adapted brain is temporarily out of balance. The mismatch between a brain "expecting" nicotine and not receiving it produces the withdrawal syndrome: irritability, craving, low mood, difficulty concentrating, sleep disturbance, increased appetite.

  • Most physical withdrawal symptoms peak in the first week and substantially resolve within 2–4 weeks — see the Hughes withdrawal time-course record R-007.
  • Craving behaves differently: it can persist for months, in waves, especially when conditioned triggers are encountered.

docs.title: Key distinction: dependence vs habit
docs.text:
Dependence Conditioned habit What it is Neuroadaptation requiring nicotine Learned associations triggering urge Timescale Resolves over weeks Weakens over months–years, by repetition Treated by NRT, varenicline, bupropion, cytisine Behavioural change, trigger management

Both matter, and they are treated differently — which is why combined medication + behavioural support outperforms either alone.

docs.title: Relapse: The Science of Returning to Smoking
Definitions first
docs.text:
• Lapse: a single slip — one cigarette or a brief episode of smoking.
  • Relapse: return to regular, ongoing smoking.
  • Abstinence: sustained non-smoking over a defined period.

Conflating lapse with relapse is a common and harmful error: it turns a single cigarette into psychological defeat, when the evidence-based response to a lapse is recommitment, not surrender.

docs.title: What the evidence says about relapse risk
docs.text:
• Relapse is most likely in the first weeks; risk declines steeply after the first months and continues to decline over years. Long-term quitters still occasionally relapse, but the base rate falls sharply.
  • Lapses are common. Many people who ultimately succeed long-term report one or more slips in their quit history — a pattern visible in the community relapse reports and consistent with the chronic-disease model of dependence (US PHS 2008).
  • Each quit attempt is informative: attempts are learning data, not moral tests. Multiple attempts are the norm — see the community question on attempt counts.

docs.title: Documented relapse contexts (from community data)
docs.text: The structured experience database documents recurring relapse contexts: alcohol and social occasions, post-lapse escalation back to full smoking, and the "just one cigarette" sequence. These are reported patterns, presented as observations — patterns section on the main site.

docs.title: What helps after a lapse (evidence-informed)
docs.text:
1. Do not extend the lapse — the single strongest predictor of full relapse is continued smoking after a slip.
  2. Analyze the trigger concretely: what cue, what time, who, what emotion.
  3. Write an if-then plan for that specific situation next time.
  4. Consider whether treatment was sufficient — unmedicated quits relapse more in trial data; discuss intensification (medication + support) if lapses recur.
  5. Restart immediately if a full relapse occurs — a new attempt is not a new identity, it is the same process with more information.

docs.title: What NOT to infer
docs.text:
• A lapse does not mean the person "cannot quit".
  • Community relapse stories are reports, not predictions of any individual's outcome.
  • Relapse is not caused by a single factor — it is a convergence of trigger, opportunity, biology and moment.

docs.title: Withdrawal: The Science
docs.text: Withdrawal is the body and brain readjusting after nicotine is removed. This section covers each major symptom: what it is, why it happens, typical timing and duration, what research documents, what varies between people, and what may help.

docs.title: The core evidence
docs.text:
The time-course is documented by the landmark Hughes review — see R-007:

  • Most physical symptoms peak in the first week and substantially resolve within 2–4 weeks.
  • Craving is the exception — it declines slowly and can persist for months in waves.
  • Symptoms vary widely between individuals in both intensity and duration.

docs.title: Symptom overview
docs.text:
Symptom Typical onset Typical duration Page Craving Immediate Weeks–months, in waves cravings Irritability Day 1–3 Peaks week 1, resolves ~2–4 weeks irritability Anxiety Day 1–3 Usually 2–4 weeks anxiety Low mood Day 1–3 Usually 2–4 weeks low-mood Sleep problems Day 1–7 Usually 2–4 weeks sleep Concentration problems Day 1–7 Usually 2–4 weeks concentration Restlessness Day 1–7 Usually 2–4 weeks restlessness Increased appetite / weight change Week 1+ Months for weight appetite-weight Cough Week 1+ Weeks–months (may transiently worsen) cough Headache Day 1–7 Usually 1–3 weeks headache Fatigue Day 1–7 Usually 2–4 weeks fatigue Constipation Week 1+ Usually 2–4 weeks constipation

Timings are typical patterns from the research literature and clinical descriptions, not guarantees — individual variation is the rule.

docs.title: Important boundary
docs.text: Withdrawal symptoms are usually mild-to-moderate and self-limiting. Some symptoms — chest pain, blood-streaked phlegm, persistent fever, severe or worsening breathlessness — are not typical withdrawal and warrant medical evaluation. The practical, plain-language version lives on the main site.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Feelings of tension, worry, nervousness or panic-like symptoms during the withdrawal period.

docs.title: Why it happens
docs.text: Nicotine withdrawal dysregulates the stress-response systems that nicotine chronically activated; quitting also removes a coping behaviour people often used to manage stress, temporarily unmasking anxiety.

docs.title: Typical timing
docs.text: Typically emerges in the first days, peaks in week 1, and settles over 2–4 weeks for most people.

docs.title: What research says
docs.text: Anxiety is documented as a withdrawal symptom (see R-007), though the effect size varies across studies. People with anxiety disorders may notice a more pronounced response early in quitting.

docs.title: What varies between people
docs.text: Wide variation: many people report calmness and relief rather than anxiety; others report notable tension. Baseline anxiety matters — someone quitting with an untreated anxiety disorder may need extra support.

docs.title: What may help
docs.text: Slow breathing exercises, reducing caffeine, physical activity, structured relaxation, and planned responses to worry spirals. Behavioural support can help distinguish withdrawal anxiety from underlying anxiety.

docs.title: When medical advice may be appropriate
docs.text:
Seek professional help for panic attacks, persistent severe anxiety lasting beyond the withdrawal window, or if anxiety prevents normal functioning.

Evidence note: withdrawal timing is drawn from the research literature (see R-007) and standard clinical descriptions. This page describes patterns, not individual predictions. Practical guidance lives on the main site withdrawal section.

docs.title: Increased Appetite and Weight Change — Withdrawal Science
Definition
docs.text: Greater hunger, snacking, taste improvement and weight gain after quitting.

docs.title: Why it happens
docs.text: Nicotine suppresses appetite and slightly raises metabolism; withdrawal reverses both. Food also substitutes for the oral habit, and taste/smell recovery makes food more rewarding. Weight gain is typically modest.

docs.title: Typical timing
docs.text: Appetite rises in the first weeks; weight gain typically occurs over the first months, with most of it in the first 3–6 months.

docs.title: What research says
docs.text: Average weight gain after quitting is commonly cited as about 4–5 kg over the first year in population studies, with wide variation — many people gain less, some more. Increased appetite is documented in R-007.

docs.title: What varies between people
docs.text: Highly variable: some people gain no weight; heavy smokers gain more on average. Fear of weight gain is a documented barrier to quitting for some groups.

docs.title: What may help
docs.text: Planning snacks (fruit, vegetables, water), keeping hands busy, building in physical activity from day one, and accepting modest weight change as vastly less harmful than continued smoking.

docs.title: When medical advice may be appropriate
docs.text:
Rapid large weight gain or disordered eating patterns deserve professional attention; also note bupropion is sometimes discussed in this context — talk to a clinician.

Evidence note: withdrawal timing is drawn from the research literature (see R-007) and standard clinical descriptions. This page describes patterns, not individual predictions. Practical guidance lives on the main site withdrawal section.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Difficulty focusing, foggy thinking and slower mental processing during early withdrawal.

docs.title: Why it happens
docs.text: Nicotine acutely enhances attention, and the adapted brain performs worse when nicotine is removed — until it re-adapts. Sleep disruption compounds the effect.

docs.title: Typical timing
docs.text: Begins within days, peaks in week 1–2, and generally resolves within 2–4 weeks.

docs.title: What research says
docs.text: Difficulty concentrating is one of the most reliably documented withdrawal symptoms (see R-007).

docs.title: What varies between people
docs.text: Office workers report this as one of the most disruptive symptoms; physical laborers often notice it less. People who used cigarettes as a focus ritual lose that cue too.

docs.title: What may help
docs.text: Breaking work into short blocks, writing lists, reducing multitasking expectations for the first weeks, staying hydrated, and protecting sleep. Remind yourself it is temporary — cognition returns to baseline.

docs.title: When medical advice may be appropriate
docs.text:
If concentration problems persist long after the withdrawal window or interfere severely, discuss with a professional — they can also reflect sleep or mood conditions.

Evidence note: withdrawal timing is drawn from the research literature (see R-007) and standard clinical descriptions. This page describes patterns, not individual predictions. Practical guidance lives on the main site withdrawal section.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Less frequent or harder bowel movements in the first weeks after quitting.

docs.title: Why it happens
docs.text: Nicotine stimulates bowel motility; its removal slows the gut temporarily. This is the inverse of the appetite increase — both reflect the gut adjusting to life without nicotine.

docs.title: Typical timing
docs.text: Typically appears in week 1–2 and resolves within 2–4 weeks.

docs.title: What research says
docs.text: Constipation is a recognized but less-studied withdrawal symptom (see R-007); gut effects are well known clinically.

docs.title: What varies between people
docs.text: People with pre-existing slow gut habits or low fiber intake notice it most; many people never experience it.

docs.title: What may help
docs.text: Water, dietary fiber, physical movement, and not ignoring the urge. Temporary use of standard fiber supplements or mild laxatives as directed is common practice.

docs.title: When medical advice may be appropriate
docs.text:
Constipation with severe pain, blood in stool, or lasting more than a few weeks warrants medical evaluation.

Evidence note: withdrawal timing is drawn from the research literature (see R-007) and standard clinical descriptions. This page describes patterns, not individual predictions. Practical guidance lives on the main site withdrawal section.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Increased coughing and phlegm production in the weeks after quitting — often called the 'quitter's cough'.

docs.title: Why it happens
docs.text: Tobacco smoke paralyzes the cilia that clean the airways. When smoke exposure stops, cilia recover and begin clearing accumulated mucus — the cough is the clean-out process, not damage.

docs.title: Typical timing
docs.text: Often appears or worsens in weeks 1–4 after quitting, then improves as airways clear; some people cough for a few months.

docs.title: What research says
docs.text: The temporal cough increase after cessation is well described clinically; lung function improvements after quitting are documented in the Surgeon General's reports.

docs.title: What varies between people
docs.text: Some people never notice it; long-term heavy smokers notice it most. The cough should progressively improve — a cough that keeps worsening beyond months needs evaluation.

docs.title: What may help
docs.text: Hydration, humidified air, and patience — it is a sign of recovery. Persistent or severe cough is not helped by resuming smoking, which restarts the damage.

docs.title: When medical advice may be appropriate
docs.text:
Cough with blood, persistent fever, chest pain, or a cough that worsens progressively for more than a few weeks warrants prompt medical evaluation.

Evidence note: withdrawal timing is drawn from the research literature (see R-007) and standard clinical descriptions. This page describes patterns, not individual predictions. Practical guidance lives on the main site withdrawal section.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: An intense urge or desire to smoke — the core symptom of nicotine dependence.

docs.title: Why it happens
docs.text: Craving has two sources: the nicotine-adapted brain signalling for nicotine (pharmacological craving), and conditioned triggers (coffee, alcohol, stress, places, routines) activating learned associations. The second source is why cravings return long after physical dependence resolves.

docs.title: Typical timing
docs.text: Cravings begin within hours of the last cigarette, peak in the first days, and occur in waves. Frequency and intensity decline over weeks, but individual cravings can still appear months later, usually when a conditioned trigger is encountered.

docs.title: What research says
docs.text: Cravings are the most persistent withdrawal symptom; the Hughes review documents that unlike most other symptoms they do not fully resolve within 2–4 weeks (see R-007). Conditioned-cue craving is well documented in cue-reactivity research.

docs.title: What varies between people
docs.text: People differ sharply: some report near-constant early craving, others report brief passing urges. Craving intensity correlates with dependence level but individual conditioning (rituals, places, people) matters more than dose.

docs.title: What may help
docs.text: Distraction, delay, drinking water, deep breathing, physical movement, and pre-planned responses to known triggers. Fast-acting NRT (gum, lozenge) targets the pharmacological component; trigger management targets the conditioned component.

docs.title: When medical advice may be appropriate
docs.text:
Cravings alone are not a medical concern, but if accompanied by chest pain, severe dizziness or symptoms suggesting another condition, seek evaluation.

Evidence note: withdrawal timing is drawn from the research literature (see R-007) and standard clinical descriptions. This page describes patterns, not individual predictions. Practical guidance lives on the main site withdrawal section.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Unusual tiredness, low energy or heavy sleepiness in early withdrawal.

docs.title: Why it happens
docs.text: Nicotine is a stimulant; withdrawal removes a chronic activation source. Sleep disruption, stress and the energy cost of brain re-adaptation all contribute.

docs.title: Typical timing
docs.text: Common in the first 1–2 weeks, improving over 2–4 weeks.

docs.title: What research says
docs.text: Fatigue is documented in withdrawal symptom research, though it overlaps with sleep and mood symptoms (see R-007).

docs.title: What varies between people
docs.text: Some people feel energized immediately; others feel drained. People quitting with anemia, thyroid conditions or poor sleep report more fatigue.

docs.title: What may help
docs.text: Prioritizing sleep, short walks (mild activity paradoxically reduces fatigue), regular meals, and temporarily reducing commitments in the first weeks.

docs.title: When medical advice may be appropriate
docs.text:
Fatigue persisting well beyond the withdrawal window, or accompanied by breathlessness, pallor, weight loss or night sweats, needs medical review.

Evidence note: withdrawal timing is drawn from the research literature (see R-007) and standard clinical descriptions. This page describes patterns, not individual predictions. Practical guidance lives on the main site withdrawal section.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Headaches in the first weeks after quitting, ranging from mild tension-type to more noticeable episodes.

docs.title: Why it happens
docs.text: Multiple mechanisms: blood flow changes as nicotine's vascular effects withdraw, caffeine-nicotine interaction changes, sleep disruption, and general stress. Nicotine is a vasoconstrictor; withdrawal changes cerebral circulation.

docs.title: Typical timing
docs.text: Usually within the first days to week, resolving over 1–3 weeks.

docs.title: What research says
docs.text: Headache is a documented though less consistently reported withdrawal symptom (see R-007).

docs.title: What varies between people
docs.text: Caffeine users who change coffee intake while quitting often trigger headaches — nicotine speeds caffeine metabolism, so the same coffee is effectively stronger after quitting.

docs.title: What may help
docs.text: Regular hydration, stable sleep, watching caffeine intake (consider slightly reducing coffee in the first weeks), and standard over-the-counter pain relief used as directed.

docs.title: When medical advice may be appropriate
docs.text:
Sudden severe headache, headache with visual changes, weakness, confusion or stiff neck needs urgent medical evaluation — these are not withdrawal.

Evidence note: withdrawal timing is drawn from the research literature (see R-007) and standard clinical descriptions. This page describes patterns, not individual predictions. Practical guidance lives on the main site withdrawal section.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Lower frustration tolerance, short temper, anger and general edginess in the first weeks after quitting.

docs.title: Why it happens
docs.text: The nicotine-adapted brain temporarily loses the calming effect of repeated nicotine dosing; combined with sleep disruption and the stress of breaking a habit, frustration tolerance drops.

docs.title: Typical timing
docs.text: Appears within 1–3 days, peaks in the first week, and typically resolves within 2–4 weeks.

docs.title: What research says
docs.text: Irritability/anger is one of the most consistently documented withdrawal symptoms in the literature (see R-007). It is rated among the most severe symptoms by people quitting.

docs.title: What varies between people
docs.text: Severity ranges from mild edginess to notable anger episodes. People with pre-existing stress or mood conditions may experience more pronounced irritability.

docs.title: What may help
docs.text: Warning family and colleagues, scheduled physical activity, adequate sleep, reducing caffeine late in the day, and giving yourself permission to step away from tense situations.

docs.title: When medical advice may be appropriate
docs.text:
If anger becomes uncontrollable, or is accompanied by severe mood disturbance or thoughts of self-harm, seek professional help — that is beyond typical withdrawal.

Evidence note: withdrawal timing is drawn from the research literature (see R-007) and standard clinical descriptions. This page describes patterns, not individual predictions. Practical guidance lives on the main site withdrawal section.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Sadness, low energy of mood, reduced interest or mild depressive feelings during withdrawal.

docs.title: Why it happens
docs.text: Removing nicotine disrupts dopamine signalling that cigarettes chronically stimulated; the brain needs time to re-regulate. Loss of a daily ritual and its social rewards also contributes.

docs.title: Typical timing
docs.text: Usually begins in the first days, is most noticeable in weeks 1–2, and improves by ~4 weeks.

docs.title: What research says
docs.text: Depressed mood is a documented withdrawal symptom (see R-007). It is distinct from clinical depression: withdrawal low mood is time-limited and resolves as neuroadaptation reverses.

docs.title: What varies between people
docs.text: People with a history of depression are at higher risk of a more pronounced low mood, and it can be hard to tell withdrawal low mood from emerging depressive relapse — an important reason to involve a professional early.

docs.title: What may help
docs.text: Maintaining routines, physical activity (with the strongest evidence for mood), social contact, realistic expectations about the first weeks, and planning pleasant activities deliberately.

docs.title: When medical advice may be appropriate
docs.text:
If low mood persists beyond a month, deepens, or includes hopelessness or thoughts of self-harm, seek professional evaluation promptly. This is a safety boundary, not a weakness.

Evidence note: withdrawal timing is drawn from the research literature (see R-007) and standard clinical descriptions. This page describes patterns, not individual predictions. Practical guidance lives on the main site withdrawal section.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: An inability to sit still, fidgeting, pacing, or a constant sense of needing to do something with the hands.

docs.title: Why it happens
docs.text: Nicotine withdrawal produces psychomotor agitation; the smoking ritual also occupied the hands and filled micro-breaks, and removing it leaves a physical void.

docs.title: Typical timing
docs.text: Early and prominent in the first week, fading over 2–4 weeks.

docs.title: What research says
docs.text: Restlessness is among the consistently measured withdrawal symptoms (see R-007).

docs.title: What varies between people
docs.text: People with strong hand-mouth rituals (smoking while working, driving, phoning) report more restlessness. Activity level also matters — moving people are less bothered.

docs.title: What may help
docs.text: Fidget substitutes (pens, stress balls), short walks, standing breaks, chewing sugar-free gum, and keeping hands busy during formerly-smoking activities.

docs.title: When medical advice may be appropriate
docs.text:
Not usually a medical concern; if accompanied by chest pain, palpitations or tremor, seek evaluation.

Evidence note: withdrawal timing is drawn from the research literature (see R-007) and standard clinical descriptions. This page describes patterns, not individual predictions. Practical guidance lives on the main site withdrawal section.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Insomnia, frequent waking, vivid dreams or daytime sleepiness in the weeks after quitting.

docs.title: Why it happens
docs.text: Nicotine is a stimulant and its withdrawal changes sleep architecture; nicotine also suppresses REM sleep, and quitting produces a rebound of vivid dreaming as REM normalizes.

docs.title: Typical timing
docs.text: Sleep disturbance typically starts in the first days, peaks in week 1, and improves over 2–4 weeks. Vivid dreams can persist longer, especially with 24-hour nicotine patch use.

docs.title: What research says
docs.text: Sleep disturbance and increased dreaming are documented withdrawal features (see R-007). Vivid dreams are also a known effect of nicotine patches worn overnight.

docs.title: What varies between people
docs.text: Some people sleep better almost immediately (no more nocturnal nicotine cravings); others struggle for weeks. Patch users who sleep poorly often benefit from removing the patch at night.

docs.title: What may help
docs.text: Consistent sleep schedule, reducing caffeine after midday, evening wind-down routines, and avoiding screens before bed. If using a 24-hour patch and dreams are disruptive, discuss patch timing with a pharmacist.

docs.title: When medical advice may be appropriate
docs.text:
Prolonged severe insomnia beyond the withdrawal window, or sleep apnea symptoms (loud snoring with pauses, daytime sleepiness), warrant medical review.

Evidence note: withdrawal timing is drawn from the research literature (see R-007) and standard clinical descriptions. This page describes patterns, not individual predictions. Practical guidance lives on the main site withdrawal section.
